title: Minimax Regret for Inequality-of-Opportunity Gini Welfare at a Population Plateau

proof_attempt_summary: Discovery delivered the matched logarithmic minimax regret order for the specified public-smoothness, known-design Bernoulli two-policy experiment, including a finite observable estimator, same-class converse, and matching sandwich on a fixed no-tie subclass. Mathematical and decision reviews passed with no findings, and the blocked Cai–Low citations were independently attested; the field novelty floor failed with a normalized incremental tier and score ceiling 6.2 below 7.4. Formalization did not run, so no Lean-verified theorem is claimed; unknown-smoothness adaptation, quantitative-margin frontiers, and practical calibration remain separate programs.
tldr: For Terschuur's IOp-Gini welfare, the bounded randomized-trial benchmark with exactly treat-all and treat-none has sharp minimax expected regret \(n^{-s/(2s+d)}\{\log(en)\}^{s/(2s+d)-1}\). The exact same order holds on the fixed subclass whose two conditional-mean pushforwards are nonatomic, so excluding all independent cross-arm pair ties leaves the minimax rate and its logarithmic factor unchanged. The same finite observable value-comparison rule attains the order on both classes; fixed prior-independent affine tilts supply the matching no-tie all-decision converse. Population plateaus and constants remain allowed in the full class, and arbitrarily small welfare gaps remain allowed in both classes. Qualitative tie exclusion therefore does not restore uniform root-\(n\) regret. These are results for the bounded randomized-trial, two-policy specialization, with no attaining upper-bound claim for the anchor's broader observational or general-policy class.
gap: IOp sign-score theory imposes tie restrictions, while the corrected nonsmooth-norm converse does not cover the H\"older endpoint. Neither delivers this full-class decision frontier \cite{Terschuur2502.13868,HanJiaoMukherjee2020}.
fill: A sharp order, including its logarithm, must be supported by a finite observable value comparison and an experiment-specific testing converse. This supplies sample-size precision for the prospective universal-provision benchmark and for opportunity-welfare comparisons, without an identification or unrestricted policy-learning claim.
